passages.text: Dyspnea during exercise and voluntary hyperpnea in women with obesity

Temporal responses of ratings of perceived breathlessness (RBP) during constant-load and incremental exercise, and during voluntary hyperpnea (EVH) were examined in obese women. Following 6min of constant-load (60W) cycling, 34 women rated RPB≥4 (+DOE) and 22 women rated RPB≤2 (−DOE). Both groups completed an incremental cycling test and an EVH test at 40 and 60L/min; RPB was assessed each minute of incremental cycling and at the end of each EVH trial. RPB increased with ventilation during constant-load (+DOE: R2=0.86; −DOE: R2=0.82) and incremental (+DOE: R2=0.91; −DOE: R2=0.92) exercise, but +DOE had a greater y-intercept than −DOE (60W: −0.16±1.53 vs −0.73±0.55; incremental: −0.50±1.40 vs −1.71±0.84). Despite matching ventilation, RPB was greater in +DOE at baseline (0.97±1.14 vs 0.14±0.28), 40L/min (2.50±1.43 vs 0.98±0.91), and 60L/min (3.94±2.19 vs 2.07±1.32) during EVH. These findings show that despite linear associations between RPB and ventilation during exercise and voluntary hyperpnea, breathlessness perception at a given ventilatory demand is heightened in +DOE compared with −DOE.

Obesity is associated with numerous health problems and exerts limitations to breathing capacity including decreased pulmonary function and altered respiratory mechanics. These effects could provoke dyspnea on exertion (−DOE), which is a very common symptom in obesity. However, not all individuals with obesity appear to experience DOE. Indeed, we have shown that during submaximal constant-load exercise, some otherwise healthy women with obesity experience dyspnea on exertion (+DOE) whereas others do not (−DOE).

At present, it remains unclear as to what mechanism(s) underlie the different ratings of perceived breathlessness (RPB; an indicator of DOE) in women with obesity. We have conducted several studies investigating possible mechanisms underlying differences between women with and without DOE, including investigations into the oxygen cost of breathing, breathing mechanics and/or breathing pattern, qualitative descriptors of respiratory sensations, fat distribution, and cardiorespiratory fitness and/or exercise capacity. However, we note that these prior studies have reported only the RPB that has been identified during the final minute of a 6 min submaximal constant-load cycling test (performed at 60 W). That is, distinctions between +DOE (RPB ≥4) and −DOE (RPB ≤2) in these prior studies are made based upon a single RPB measurement during exercise at the same absolute work rate. Thus, the dynamic adjustment of RPB, either as a function of changes in relative exercise intensity or changes in ventilatory demand over time, has not been investigated in women with obesity. Given the temporal dynamics of respiratory sensations, it could be even more important to investigate the dynamic response of RPB. Indeed, investigating the dynamic response of RPB could be more representative of the individual’s perception of the overall exercise/ventilatory challenge, provide important insights into the origins of the dyspneic sensations, and/or help explain why some otherwise healthy women with obesity experience DOE and others do not. Moreover, it is currently unknown whether the dynamic response of RPB with exercise is related to exercise intensity, ventilatory demand, or a combination of both in women with obesity.

Therefore, the purpose of the present study was to explore the dynamic response of RBP during constant-load and incremental exercise, as well as at various levels of eucapnic voluntary hyperpnea (EVH). We assessed RPB during EVH to negate any potential confounding influence of exercise intensity on sensations of dyspnea when ventilatory demand was elevated. We retrospectively evaluated subjects’ RPB throughout both submaximal constant-load and incremental exercise (during which ventilation [] was changing continuously), as well as at similar ventilatory demands during EVH in the same large group of participants as we have reported on previously.
